summary: 12 finding(s) across 4 file(s): 1 blocker, 3 high, 5 medium, 1 low, 2 info. 3 rule(s) depend on APIs missing from your QNX SDP 8.0.0 sysroot. Detected roles: device service, periodic control loop, daemon, ipc server. Recommended shape on QNX: a /dev/vitals_monitor resource manager driven by a pulse timer. Readiness score 19/100 (deterministic formula).

findings.title: Linux i2c-dev
findings.guidance: QNX I2C controllers are served by board-specific resource-manager drivers controlled with devctl() (see <hw/i2c.h> in your SDP for the command set). Wrap sensor access in a HAL and implement the QNX side against your board's I2C driver.

findings.title: eventfd notifier
findings.guidance: eventfd is used here as a thread-to-loop wake-up. On QNX a pulse sent to the loop's channel does the same job without a file descriptor, and carries a code and a value. A pipe is the portable fallback.
findings.sysroot_detail: eventfd: not exported by any sysroot library; <sys/eventfd.h> not in sysroot

findings.title: Root-only daemon / Linux capabilities
findings.guidance: QNX splits root's power into abilities. Start as root only long enough to do the privileged setup (for example registering a path name), then call procmgr_ability() to keep just the abilities you need, lock the rest, and switch to an unprivileged user. A secpol policy can express the same thing declaratively.

alternatives.note: Retain only named abilities, then drop root.

findings.title: Linux /sys paths
findings.guidance: There is no sysfs on QNX. PWM, GPIO and thermal data come from board-specific resource managers. Hide these behind a HAL and implement the QNX backend for your board's drivers.

findings.title: Host-only compiler settings
findings.guidance: Cross-compile with qcc/q++ and a -V variant (gcc_ntox86_64, gcc_ntoaarch64le). Remove host-only flags such as -march=native and hardcoded gcc, and do not fail the build when CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME is not Linux. The kit's toolchain file sets all of this.

findings.title: fork() in a multithreaded program
findings.guidance: posix_spawn() is the recommended way to start processes on QNX. fork() in a multithreaded program is unsafe under POSIX on any OS, because only the calling thread is copied and locks held by other threads stay locked in the child.

alternatives.note: Create the child in one call; no copy of the parent's address space.

findings.title: ioctl on device descriptors
findings.guidance: QNX offers ioctl() as a wrapper over devctl() for common requests, but driver-specific requests must be rewritten against the QNX driver's DCMD_* set. Wrap device access in a small hardware-abstraction layer (HAL) so the Linux and QNX implementations can live side by side.

alternatives.note: Driver-specific DCMD_* commands; check the driver for your board.
Introduce a HAL interface around device access.

findings.title: Linux-only link libraries
findings.guidance: On QNX the pthread, real-time and dynamic-loading functions are part of libc. Drop a -l flag only if that library is missing from the sysroot (the audit checks this). In CMake prefer find_package(Threads) + Threads::Threads.
findings.sysroot_detail: not in sysroot lib dirs: librt (provided by libc on QNX)

findings.title: systemd unit / watchdog script

findings.guidance: QNX targets have no systemd. Start the service from the image's startup script (or SLM where available), daemonize with procmgr_daemon(), and supervise daemon processes using procmgr_event_notify_add(PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH, ...) (or HAM where the optional High Availability package is installed).

alternatives.note: Process manager daemon death notifications and supervisor restart loop.

findings.title: sleep-based periodic loop
findings.guidance: A relative sleep inside a loop drifts by the loop body's run time. Use clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, ...) with a running deadline, or a pulse timer when the thread also needs to receive other events.

alternatives.note: Pulse timer when the loop also receives messages.

findings.title: syslog logging
findings.guidance: syslog() works on QNX. slog2 (slog2_register, slog2f) is recommended for structured, low-overhead logs that you can read with slog2info.

findings.title: POSIX shared memory
findings.guidance: shm_open()/mmap() work on QNX. For memory shared with devices or across a hypervisor boundary, look at typed memory (posix_typed_mem_open). Keep the shared struct layout fixed-size and guard it with a process-shared, priority-inheriting mutex.

alternatives.note: POSIX shared memory; typed memory for physical regions.

benefits.title: Predictable timing for time-critical work
benefits.why: vitals_monitor has timing-sensitive code (a periodic control loop; sleep-based periodic loop in src/vitals.c:79). On a general-purpose Linux kernel, exactly when that code runs depends on everything else the system is doing. QNX is a hard real-time OS: the highest-priority ready thread always runs, timers can deliver a pulse straight to the waiting thread, mutexes and message passing use priority inheritance, and run-masks can keep a core free for the critical thread, so timing stays predictable when the system is busy.
benefits.evidence_summary: a periodic control loop; sleep-based periodic loop in src/vitals.c:79

benefits.title: A driver or service crash does not take the system down
benefits.why: vitals_monitor works with hardware (opens Linux device files under /dev; Linux i2c-dev in src/vitals.c:25). On Linux, device drivers run inside the kernel, so a driver bug can bring down the whole machine. In QNX the kernel only schedules, passes messages and handles interrupts; drivers and services such as vitals_monitor run as ordinary processes with their own memory protection. If one fails, the kernel and the other processes keep running and the failed process can be restarted.
benefits.evidence_summary: opens Linux device files under /dev; Linux i2c-dev in src/vitals.c:25

benefits.title: Automatic detection and restart when a process dies
benefits.capability: Process-manager death notifications (and HAM where installed)
benefits.why: vitals_monitor relies on Linux supervision (runs as a background daemon; systemd unit / watchdog script in scripts/vitals-watchdog.sh:1; fork() in a multithreaded program in src/vitals.c:87). On QNX a small guardian can register for PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH and receive a kernel pulse the moment the daemon exits, then restart it with posix_spawn(); because services are isolated processes, restarting one does not disturb the others.
benefits.evidence_summary: runs as a background daemon; systemd unit / watchdog script in scripts/vitals-watchdog.sh:1; fork() in a multithreaded program in src/vitals.c:87

benefits.title: Run without full root rights
benefits.capability: Fine-grained process abilities and security policies
benefits.why: vitals_monitor currently needs elevated rights (root-only daemon / Linux capabilities in src/vitals.c:17; POSIX shared memory in src/vitals.c:109). QNX splits root's power into individual abilities (for example: create a /dev entry, raise thread priority, map physical memory). With procmgr_ability() the service keeps only the abilities it needs, locks them, and then runs as a normal user; secpol policies can enforce the same rules system-wide. A compromised service can then do far less damage.
benefits.evidence_summary: root-only daemon / Linux capabilities in src/vitals.c:17; POSIX shared memory in src/vitals.c:109

benefits.title: Fast, priority-aware communication between processes
benefits.capability: Synchronous message passing as the core of the OS
benefits.why: vitals_monitor coordinates work through Linux event and IPC mechanisms (serves other processes (Unix sockets, message queues or shared memory); eventfd notifier in src/vitals.c:14; POSIX shared memory in src/vitals.c:109). In QNX, message passing is how the whole OS works: a client's MsgSend() copies data directly into the server, blocks until the reply, and the server temporarily runs at the client's priority. Clients can also simply open() and read() a /dev/vitals_monitor path. This gives one consistent, priority-aware way to talk between components.
benefits.evidence_summary: serves other processes (Unix sockets, message queues or shared memory); eventfd notifier in src/vitals.c:14; POSIX shared memory in src/vitals.c:109

benefits.title: A path to functional-safety certification
benefits.why: vitals_monitor looks like embedded control or device software (a periodic control loop; opens Linux device files under /dev; Linux i2c-dev in src/vitals.c:25). If it ever has to meet a functional safety standard (automotive, industrial or medical), QNX offers a safety-certified variant of the OS, which removes a large part of the work compared with arguing the safety of a general-purpose kernel. Your own application still needs its own safety process.
benefits.evidence_summary: a periodic control loop; opens Linux device files under /dev; Linux i2c-dev in src/vitals.c:25

benefits.title: See exactly what the system did, and when
benefits.capability: Kernel event tracing and structured system logging
benefits.why: vitals_monitor relies on Linux logging or /proc inspection (syslog logging in src/vitals.c:39; sleep-based periodic loop in src/vitals.c:79). QNX's tracelogger records kernel events (thread switches, messages, interrupts) with timestamps, which shows exactly why a deadline was missed; slog2 gives fast, structured logs that stay readable after a crash.
benefits.evidence_summary: syslog logging in src/vitals.c:39; sleep-based periodic loop in src/vitals.c:79

benefits.title: Most of the code carries over
benefits.why: QNX implements the POSIX APIs this code already relies on (threads, timers, sockets, files), so the port is about the Linux-only parts listed in the audit rather than a rewrite. The audit found 12 Linux-specific pattern(s) across 4 file(s); the readiness score is 19/100.

qnx_fit.headline: Strong fit: vitals_monitor does the kind of real-time, device or service work QNX is built for.
reasons: A driver or service crash does not take the system down
Automatic detection and restart when a process dies
caveats: Porting effort: 4 blocker/high finding(s) need code changes first (see the Audit tab and the step-by-step guide).
Hardware access depends on your board's QNX drivers: CAN, I2C and SPI interfaces differ from Linux.
These are capabilities QNX provides, not measurements. Use the Verify tab on a QNX target before relying on timing.

pillar1_features.rationale: `src/vitals.c` owns a device and a processing loop. On QNX that is naturally a resource manager: it registers /dev/vitals_monitor in the path space, clients use plain open/read/ write/devctl, and every request arrives as a message that inherits the client's priority. Device access moves out of client code into one process that can be restarted on its own.
pillar1_features.diagram_mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C1["client: open + devctl"] -->|"MsgSend, client priority"| R["/dev/vitals_monitor resource manager"]
  T["timer pulse"] --> R
  R --> D["device driver resmgr"]

pillar1_features.rationale: `src/vitals.c` multiplexes timers, notifications and I/O in a Linux event loop. A QNX channel replaces it: each source sends a pulse with its own code and priority, and a single receive call hands them to the thread in priority order.
pillar1_features.diagram_mermaid:
flowchart LR
  TM["timer_create, SIGEV_PULSE"] -->|"code TIMER, prio 30"| CH(("channel"))
  W["worker thread"] -->|"MsgSendPulse, code FLUSH"| CH
  IO["ionotify on fd"] -->|"code IO"| CH
  CH --> L["MsgReceivePulse loop"]

pillar1_features.rationale: `src/vitals.c` runs as root throughout. procmgr_ability() keeps only the abilities the service still needs after start-up and locks the rest before dropping to a service user.
The same least-privilege intent can be written as a secpol policy for vitals_monitor, so the system integrator controls abilities without changing code.

`scripts/vitals-watchdog.sh` relies on systemd or scripts for restarts. On QNX 8.0, procmgr_daemon() and procmgr_event_notify_add(PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH) notify a guardian via kernel pulse immediately on process termination (or use HAM when the optional HA package is installed).
pillar1_features.diagram_mermaid:
flowchart LR
  S["vitals_monitor daemon"] -->|"PROCMGR_EVENT_DAEMON_DEATH pulse"| G["procmgr / guardian"]
  G -->|"posix_spawn restart"| S

pillar1_features.rationale: Capture a kernel event trace with tracelogger while vitals_monitor runs and inspect scheduling, IPC and interrupts in the System Profiler (Momentics or the VS Code QNX Toolkit) to confirm the timing behaviour after porting.
`src/vitals.c` logs through syslog. slog2 gives per-buffer verbosity and very low overhead in time-critical paths, and slog2info reads the buffers on the target.
`src/vitals.c` publishes data in shared memory. POSIX shm works on QNX; typed memory is available when the region must map to specific physical memory.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Sensor reads use Linux i2c-dev request codes directly.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A sensor HAL isolates the bus driver; the QNX backend uses the board's I2C resource manager.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: An eventfd wake-up carries no payload and no priority; the receiver must read shared state separately to learn what happened.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A pulse carries an 8-bit code and a 32-bit value plus the sender's priority, so the receiver knows what happened and the scheduler orders the work correctly.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: The process runs with full root privileges for its whole lifetime.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: procmgr_ability() keeps only the abilities the service needs and locks them, so a compromise does not yield root.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Child processes are created with fork() from a threaded parent.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: posix_spawn() creates the child directly and can set its scheduling policy and priority.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Device control calls are scattered through application code and tied to Linux request codes.
pillar2_improvements.qnx_improvement: A HAL with a devctl()-based QNX backend isolates board-specific commands in one file.

pillar2_improvements.current_limitation: Restart policy lives in systemd or a cron script, which QNX targets do not have.

# QNX SDP 8.0 CMake toolchain file - generated by QNX Integration Advisor for vitals-monitor.
# Usage:
#   source ~/qnx800/qnxsdp-env.sh
#   cmake -B build-qnx -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=cmake/qnx8-toolchain.cmake -DQNX_ARCH=x86_64
#   cmake --build build-qnx

if(NOT DEFINED ENV{QNX_TARGET} OR NOT DEFINED ENV{QNX_HOST})
  message(FATAL_ERROR "QNX_TARGET/QNX_HOST are not set. Source qnxsdp-env.sh from your SDP 8.0 install first.")
endif()

set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME QNX)
set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_VERSION 8.0.0)

if(NOT DEFINED QNX_ARCH)
  set(QNX_ARCH x86_64)
endif()

if(QNX_ARCH STREQUAL "x86_64")
  set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR x86_64)
  set(_qnx_variant gcc_ntox86_64)
elseif(QNX_ARCH STREQUAL "aarch64le")
  set(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR aarch64)
  set(_qnx_variant gcc_ntoaarch64le)
else()
  message(FATAL_ERROR "Unsupported QNX_ARCH '${QNX_ARCH}' (use x86_64 or aarch64le)")
endif()

# qcc selects the target with -V<variant>; CMake passes COMPILER_TARGET as -V for qcc.
set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER qcc)
set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER_TARGET ${_qnx_variant})
set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER q++)
set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_TARGET ${_qnx_variant}_cxx)

set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH $ENV{QNX_TARGET} $ENV{QNX_TARGET}/${QNX_ARCH})
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PROGRAM NEVER)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_LIBRARY ONLY)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_INCLUDE ONLY)
set(CMAKE_FIND_ROOT_PATH_MODE_PACKAGE ONLY)

kit.description: mkqnximage QEMU target + copy binaries over SSH
kit.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Build and boot a QNX 8.0 QEMU target with mkqnximage, then copy the kit binaries to it.
# Generated by QNX Integration Advisor for vitals-monitor.
# Prerequisites: QNX SDP 8.0 with mkqnximage, QEMU, `source qnxsdp-env.sh`, an SSH key.
# Check `mkqnximage --help` for the exact options in your SDP patch level.
set -eu

ARCH=${ARCH:-x86_64}
VM_DIR=${VM_DIR:-$HOME/qnx-advisor-vm}
SSH_PUB=${SSH_PUB:-$HOME/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub}
KIT_DIR=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)

command -v mkqnximage >/dev/null || { echo "mkqnximage not found: source qnxsdp-env.sh first" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$SSH_PUB" ] || { echo "SSH public key $SSH_PUB not found (set SSH_PUB)" >&2; exit 1; }

mkdir -p "$VM_DIR"
cd "$VM_DIR"
if [ ! -d output ]; then
    echo "== building QEMU image in $VM_DIR"
    mkqnximage --type=qemu --arch="$ARCH" --ssh-ident="$SSH_PUB"
fi

echo "== starting VM (headless)"
mkqnximage --run=-h &
sleep 5

IP=""
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
    IP=$(mkqnximage --getip 2>/dev/null || true)
    [ -n "$IP" ] && break
    sleep 2
done
[ -n "$IP" ] || { echo "could not get VM IP" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "== VM at $IP"

make -C "$KIT_DIR" -f Makefile.qnx ARCH="$ARCH"
scp -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new "$KIT_DIR"/build/"$ARCH"/* qnxuser@"$IP":/data/home/qnxuser/
echo "== copied kit binaries to /data/home/qnxuser on $IP"
echo "   ssh qnxuser@$IP"
echo "   then: su -c '/data/home/qnxuser/vitals_monitor_resmgr -u 1000 &' && /data/home/qnxuser/vitals_monitorctl"

# Advanced / optional: mkifs buildfile fragment for vitals-monitor.
# For QEMU and VMs prefer mkqnximage (target/run-qemu.sh). Merge this fragment into a
# board buildfile from your BSP if you build a custom image.

[+script] .vitals_monitor-start = {
    /proc/boot/vitals_monitor_resmgr -p 1 -u 1000 &
    waitfor /dev/vitals_monitor 5
}

[perms=0755] /proc/boot/vitals_monitor_resmgr = build/x86_64/vitals_monitor_resmgr
[perms=0755] /proc/boot/vitals_monitorctl = build/x86_64/vitals_monitorctl
